strengths: introduces a novel perspective on noise in deep learning by categorizing it into positive noise (PN) and harmful noise (HN) based on its impact on task complexity
offers a fresh approach to understanding noise in the context of deep learning
The proposed method is effective and well explained.
It works with popular architectures. CNN and Transformers show in the paper.
The method is helpful in domain adaptation as well.
Theoretical analysis is provided to characterize the idea of 'positive noise' proposed in this paper.
Empirical experiments are given in this paper to support the advantage of leveraging positive noise.
The approach 'NoisyNN' that utilizes the positive noise is proposed in this paper, and its efficacy is demonstrated through empirical experiments.
The analysis of noise choices is thorough including Linear transformation noise, Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise.
The method can be generalized to various architecture includes ResNet and ViT.
weaknesses: It is inconvenient to reproduce the experimental results without the pretrained models; the authors should provide models or APIs to make replication easier.
Paper compares the proposed approach only with 2 basic latent dimension noise; approaches similar to Manifold mixup such as Noisy Feature Mixup should be compared.
Performance drops when combined with input augmentations (Table 17), which is problematic because input augmentations are a staple of training neural networks.
It is unclear how the method compares against advanced input augmentations (like mixup, cutmix, RandAugment, etc.) and whether it is compatible with them.
The paper's claim can be strengthened by showing results with another linear transformation noise.
The idea of the paper is demonstrated only with a specific type of positive noise (positive linear transformation noise); it is unclear how it works with other types of positive noise.
The current theoretical analysis is primarily for classification tasks; it is unclear how it can be extended to cover other related tasks mentioned in the paper.
Poor writing organization; the authors should emphasize that the proposed NoisyNN is built upon linear transformation noise to avoid confusion.
Experimental details are not explained clearly.
The authors should reference the codebase/implementation of the baseline when reporting results such as Vanilla ViT-B accuracy of 84.33%.
It is unclear whether the noises are applied to the ImageNet-1K fine‑tuning or to ImageNet-21K pretraining plus ImageNet-1K fine‑tuning.
The specifics of injecting noise at the feature or feature‑grid level are unclear; it is not stated whether noise is applied to each feature grid individually.
Comparison with state‑of‑the‑art data augmentation models is missing; related work only covers research up to 2020 and Table 18 uses overly simplistic baselines.
Suspicious claim of 94.8% top‑1 accuracy on ImageNet‑1K, which exceeds known state‑of‑the‑art performance and raises concerns about the validity of the results.
The README in the anonymous repository is entirely missing, making reproducibility difficult; clear instructions and a complete codebase are needed.
